So to give you a little bit of an overview here, the state of Washington currently has over 13,000 sites on the Washington Department of Ecology Confirmed and Suspected Contaminated Sites list. Of those, 36 are in Lakewood. Also, 18 contaminated sites have been cleaned up and taken off this list. Sites may take many, many years to clean up. It depends largely on the contaminants as well as the extent of the contamination and whether or not there is motivation to clean those sites. Typically, that is due to a sale. Property owner wants to sell their property or redevelop it. City is concerned both on soil and groundwater contamination and the spread of that contamination and the threat to the environment and to human health. There are basically three types of sites here in Lakewood. The first is the Superfund site, which is an uncontrolled or abandoned site. Typically, it is monitored by the federal government. These are typically more severe than a typical brownfield site. Lakewood has two such sites. One, the American Lake Gardens site in Woodbrook. This one was due to the Air Force disposal of waste during the 1940s to the 1970s. This one has been removed from the list and it just continues to be monitored over time. The second one is the Lakewood ponders site. This site is currently on the list. It is due to contaminants being released from a previous plaza dry cleaners. Solvents were dumped into a bottomless or bottomless USTs or underground storage tanks. That site has been cleaned up. Lakewood water has installed some significant equipment, which I'll talk a little bit more about in a few minutes. This is located on the east side of I-5 off of New York Avenue. There's also brownfield sites, which are most of our sites here in Lakewood. Brownfields are those sites that present potentially hazardous contaminants, which may complicate reuse or expansion or redevelopment of sites. Those sites are monitored by the Washington Department of Ecology. Within the brownfield sites, there are also USTs, what we call underground storage tank sites. Those have contaminants mostly from petroleum, other chemicals, heating oils, kerosene, and other types of chemicals like that. Those sites are monitored by the Tacoma Pierce County Health Department. Those sites are typically, I would say about 90% of all of our brownfield sites have some type of UST or petroleum or hazardous materials such as that. Most of the sites, too, that we're looking at here in Lakewood are due to gas stations, dry cleaners, or auto-related repairs and maintenance sites or spills that occur. Contaminants that we most likely are to see are lead, petroleum, asbestos, also coal, soot, contaminants from fires, also from manufacturing byproducts, other metals, as well as degreasers, other solvents, as I mentioned, dry cleaners, and also lubricants, paints, and arsenic. I'm going to briefly go through the sites that we have here in Lakewood to give you an idea of what we're looking at. First of all, there are a couple of acronyms I wanted to point out to you guys. An owner may opt to go through the PLEA in order to clean up the sites, or they may join the BCP. NFA means no further action, and that means the owner has met a cleanup target, and the government doesn't consider those sites worthy of additional attention.
